title: Getting Students to Share Their Half-Formed Gray Mist
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer builds his argument around a distinction offered by tutoring researcher Mike Goldstein: human tutors succeed largely by drawing out a student's half-formed gray-mist idea so it can be clarified, whereas AI tutors are excellent explainers but students simply will not reveal their half-formed misunderstandings to a chatbot the way they will to a trusted human. Meyer illustrates the point with fifth-grade teacher Itzel Silva, who uses Spanish and embodied gesture to draw a bilingual student's partial understanding of parallel lines into full articulation, arguing this is a distinctly human, relationship-dependent teaching move that current AI tutoring cannot replicate. He extends the argument into a challenge for school leaders, framing the real question not as will AI eventually match this but as a comparison between a speculative technological bet and the proven, immediate value of investing in teacher practice like Silva's. The piece closes with reader comments critiquing AI-driven models for narrowing what counts as school, situating his argument within an ongoing debate about AI's role in classroom pedagogy.
points: Meyer's central pedagogical claim, sourced from tutoring researcher Mike Goldstein, is that AI tutors are strong explainers but students won't reveal a half-formed gray-mist misunderstanding to a chatbot the way they will to a trusted human tutor.

The Itzel Silva classroom example, using Spanish and embodied gesture to coax out a bilingual student's partial understanding of parallel lines, grounds the abstract claim in a concrete, replicable teaching move.
Meyer reframes the AI-tutoring debate for school leaders as a choice between a speculative bet about the future and the needs of students and the capacities of teachers now.
A featured reader comment extends the critique of AI-driven models, arguing such programs narrow school to primarily math while sidelining humanities and social-skill development.
quotes: I think people often misconceive of tutoring as explaining. Sometimes that's true, hey today we're going to learn about photosynthesis, but a lot of times you're trying to get the kid to blurt out the half-formed gray-mist idea in their head so that you can help clarify. They're sort of stuck and you get them unstuck.
AI is a very good explainer, but the behavior we see in randomized trials so far is the kid simply will not reveal their misunderstanding to the AI.

Silva knows the student speaks Spanish and also notices the student using her arms to describe skew lines, lines that meet. Silva wants to draw out the student's half-formed gray-mist ideas about parallel lines so she uses the languages the student seems to speak comfortably, both Spanish and embodied, to clarify parallel lines.

If you're a school leader, I think you can ask yourself a couple of interesting questions here. You can ask yourself, at what point in the future will chatbot tutors offer my students even 5% of what Silva has offered her students?

The entrenched hostility in tech land to teachers is so strange and deep, is it just because it's a care profession? Because it has soft skills they don't like? Why is that the job that they're so keen to put on the chopping block?
We're seeing more and more schools succeed by leveraging technology thoughtfully. But that success is never about the technology alone. The teachers and administrators deserve most of the credit.
